items.title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.original_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_description: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer Claims ITL Editorial Team Tue, 10/06/2026 - 11:19 Chief claims officers must transform their departments into AI-native ground-truth engines or risk becoming the bottleneck in enterprise transformation. October 7, 2026 Image For decades, the mandate of the chief claims cfficer was relatively clear: build a strong organization to investigate claims, control costs, manage litigation, negotiate settlements, and deliver fair outcomes. That mandate is no longer sufficient. The 2027 chief claims officer has a much bigger job: build the insurer's ground-truth engine—an AI-native operation that produces superior outcomes, industrializes negotiation excellence, and converts what claims learns into intelligence for the entire enterprise. This is not simply about using AI to make legacy claims processes more efficient. AI is turning insurance into an information business—and the most important ground truth in that business is generated in claims. Claims reveal what actually happened to the risks the insurer underwrote, what drove the loss, and what ultimately determined its economic outcome. To compete in an AI world, insurers will need to capture that ground truth, make it machine-readable, and use it to improve underwriting, pricing, reserving, and portfolio management. That puts claims—and the chief claims officer—on the front line of this unprecedented transformation. A new competitive environment Claims officers in traditional claims organizations face urgent and pressing competition from two sources at once. On one side is an increasingly industrialized plaintiff bar. On the other side is a new generation of AI-native insurers, poised to move forward. On the first side, consider Morgan & Morgan. The personal-injury giant says it has invested roughly $300 million in technology and AI and plans at least $1 billion more over the next decade. Its proprietary MX2 platform supports medical-record extraction, case research, document generation, demand letters, and trial preparation, while Injury.com digitally acquires and qualifies potential claims. Private equity is adding fuel, investing in personal-injury platforms to scale technology, analytics, marketing and standardized operations. The plaintiff bar is turning claim development and negotiation from individual craftsmanship into an industrial system. On the second side, a new generation of AI-native insurers is being built without decades of legacy technology, workflows and organizational baggage. Companies such as Corgi are attempting to build insurance businesses from inception around modern data architectures, AI agents and technology-speed iteration. McKinsey has warned that AI-native insurance businesses can increasingly build and refine products in weeks while incumbents remain calibrated to annual planning cycles and multi-year transformations. Legacy insurers are being squeezed from both directions: out-innovated by the plaintiff bar in the contest over outcomes and potentially out-architected by AI-native insurers in the contest over how insurance itself operates. Claims sits directly in the middle. That changes the requirements of its leader. 1. Level the playing field with the plaintiff bar The plaintiff bar has largely approached AI as a weapon for improving economic outcomes. Carriers have largely approached it as a tool for workflow efficiency. AI-powered demand packages are working. Carriers are only beginning to experiment seriously with the corresponding AI-powered offer package. Meanwhile, sophisticated plaintiff organizations are accumulating data, developing proprietary AI and attracting enormous capital. The plaintiff bar is both the threat and the proof point. They are investing their own money—and increasing institutional capital—because better case development, persuasion, and negotiation improve their economics. The CCO must build institutional capabilities that can match increasingly industrialized counterparties. 2. Institutionalize negotiation excellence Most carriers have some excellent negotiators. That is no longer enough. If negotiation materially affects indemnity outcomes, it cannot remain an individual skill distributed unevenly across thousands of claims professionals. The organization should know who its elite negotiators are, why they outperform and how those behaviors can be replicated. Carriers that cannot identify, measure and reproduce negotiation excellence do not really possess a negotiation capability. They possess individual negotiators. The CCO must turn individual excellence into measurable institutional capability. 3. Stop putting AI band-aids on pre-AI claims operations Many carriers can produce an impressive list of AI-centric projects: summarize a file, extract information, draft correspondence, analyze a demand, route work, search notes, or give adjusters Copilot. Those applications can create real value. But old process plus an AI tool means slightly better old process. McKinsey has warned about layering new technology onto legacy insurance operating models. BCG similarly distinguishes between deploying AI into existing processes and reshaping workflows around AI. The CCO must redesign the operating model, not merely automate the existing one. 4. Build machine-first claims The traditional claim file was built primarily for humans. Documents, notes, emails, medical records, and litigation materials accumulate while experienced professionals gradually construct an understanding of what happened. In an AI-native operation, every claim should progressively become a machine-readable representation of the claim—the people, events, evidence, injuries, allegations, relationships, negotiations and outcomes. That structured claim becomes the substrate on which specialized AI agents can continuously reason. Instead of occasionally asking AI to summarize a file, machines continuously read, structure, monitor, compare, detect, and prepare. The CCO must make claims machine-readable while elevating, not diminishing, human judgment and action. 5. Build and lead a hybrid workforce The future claim officer will have two kinds of capacity at their disposal: human expertise and machine intelligence. AI agents will increasingly read, structure, monitor, research, compare, detect, analyze and prepare. Humans will increasingly concentrate on judgment, investigation, strategy, creativity, empathy, supervision, accountability and negotiation. That will make exceptional claims professionals more important, not less. Imagine an elite negotiator supported by agents that continuously understand the evidence, medical history, venue, plaintiff counsel, negotiation history, and comparable outcomes. The machine handles much of the cognitive preparation. The human concentrates on what exceptional humans do best: think, strategize, persuade, read the counterparty, exercise judgment, and negotiate. The CCO must become the architect of human and machine capacity—designing how each works together to produce better outcomes. 6. Make every negotiation a learning event A sophisticated plaintiff demand should eventually meet an equally sophisticated carrier response. But the bigger opportunity comes afterward. Every demand, analysis, strategy, offer, response, counteroffer, and outcome must become institutional knowledge in the same way that the plaintiff bar is institutionalizing these events. Which plaintiff firms consistently outperform? Which strategies work against them? Which facts change settlement value? Which negotiators outperform expectations? Where does the organization systematically overpay? Every negotiation should make the next negotiation smarter. The CCO must ensure every claim and negotiation makes the organization smarter. 7. Elevate claims into the insurer's ground-truth engine This is where the transformation extends beyond claims. Underwriting begins with hypotheses about risk. Pricing quantifies them. Reserving updates them. Claims discovers what was actually true. Claims learns what caused the loss, how injuries developed, what evidence mattered, how attorneys behaved, which defenses and negotiation strategies worked, and what the risk ultimately cost. Yet much of that knowledge remains trapped in PDFs, notes, litigation files and the heads of experienced claims professionals. Claims should continuously produce structured intelligence that flows into underwriting, pricing, reserving, risk, reinsurance and portfolio management. The claim is no longer simply something to resolve and close. It is one of the insurer's richest proprietary information assets. The CCO must turn claims knowledge into enterprise intelligence—making the claims organization the feedback loop that allows the entire enterprise to learn. 8. Don't let claims become the transformation bottleneck This may be the requirement that matters most to the rest of the C-suite. A legacy insurer can modernize distribution, underwriting, pricing and portfolio management. But if its richest source of ground truth remains trapped inside a document-centric, human-first claims operation moving through multi-year transformation cycles, the rest of the enterprise eventually hits a wall. AI-native competitors do not have to unwind decades of organizational architecture before redesigning how humans, machines and data work together. Incumbents do. That makes speed itself a competitive capability. The modern CCO must protect the integrity of a massive, consequential operation while simultaneously making it capable of continuous change. The plaintiff bar is moving at technology speed. AI-native competitors are being built for technology speed. Claims cannot continue moving at insurance speed. The CCO must ensure claims leads rather than constrains the insurer's AI transformation. The mandate has changed None of these requirements eliminates the traditional responsibilities of the CCO. Claims still must be handled fairly; customers, regulatory obligations, litigation, reserves and operational discipline still matter. But those responsibilities are increasingly table stakes. Sophisticated plaintiff organizations are industrializing the pursuit of settlement dollars while AI-native insurers are being architected as technology-speed information businesses. Between them sits a claims organization that, at many incumbents, was designed for another era. That creates both a threat and an extraordinary opportunity. Carriers that generate that ground truth better, negotiate from it more effectively, make it machine-readable and distribute it throughout the enterprise will possess something more valuable than a more efficient claims department. They will possess a continuously learning insurance enterprise. As chief claims officers enter 2027, the question is no longer whether their departments will use more AI. It is whether they can transform their departments into a competitive advantage rather than the bottleneck preventing the enterprise from changing with it. Taylor Smith John Burge

items.rss_description: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation Customer Experience ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/14/2026 - 13:12 Gen Z's demand for instant digital experiences is forcing insurers to modernize claims payments or risk losing policyholders. October 15, 2026 Image As digital natives who've grown up tethered to smartphones and social media, the Gen Z population's effect on today's consumer trends is well documented . Young shoppers' demands for instant gratification in consumer transactions have ushered in an era of in-app shopping, next-day shipping, and fast, friction-free digital payment options. Gen Z's influence is extending to the insurance claims process, as well. More and more, Gen Z's preferences are pushing the industry to uplevel its claims experience – to make it faster, more convenient, more tied to mobile, and more transparent to the policyholder. InvoiceCloud's 2026 Claims Experience survey of 1,000 U.S. policyholders shows Gen Z is nearly twice as likely as the overall population to prefer a digital wallet for claims payments (13% versus 7%). Recent research shines a light on policyholders' discontent with what they identify as their biggest deal breaker: an unacceptably slow process for paying claims. The InvoiceCloud survey found that only 9% of policyholders received their claims payment within two days. Meanwhile, a quarter of respondents say it took more than a week to receive their claims payout, while an unfortunate 13% waited "several weeks" to get these urgent funds. This could cause ripple effects. In a 2022 report, " Transforming claims and underwriting with AI ", Accenture estimated that poor claims experiences could put up to $170 billion in global insurance premiums at risk through 2027. The InvoiceCloud survey shows how these risks could materialize. At least 75% of policyholders surveyed say they would consider switching carriers after a single negative claims experience. That's a high percentage in any field, but it's particularly high in personal-lines P&C, where switching providers is often easier than it is in commercial, E&S, or other specialty markets. Improving the claims process How do insurance carriers improve the claims process? Our research found that speed and transparency matter most of all to policyholders. When asked directly, 30% named a faster claims payment after approval as the single change they want most, more than any other option, while 22% preferred clearer status communication. Gen Z echoes that second point: 24% named clearer, more consistent communication about payment status as the one change they would make, on par with the 21% who named faster payment. Another issue: Many carriers have modernized inbound premium payments, but outbound disbursements still rely on paper checks and manual processing. Paper checks create fraud risk, delivery problems, and extra work for commissions and return premiums. The next generation of policyholders is demanding two changes to this payment structure. They prefer a shift to digital, and they want choices. Digital disbursement platforms can support a wide variety of options including ACH/direct deposit, debit cards, virtual cards, and digital wallets. Direct deposit to a bank account is policyholders' favorite payout, preferred by 52% of respondents, more than all other options combined. Printed checks still account for 19%, likely reflecting legacy carrier processes rather than genuine preference. The gap between generations is wide: 32% of Baby Boomers prefer a printed check, compared with just 9% of Gen Z. If slow payouts can lead to defections, digital insurance payments can operate as a retention tool. Insurance carriers can do this by ensuring this critical touchpoint becomes an easy experience end-to-end, from allowing policyholders to self-serve through digital premium payments, paperless billing, and automatic payments, to instant disbursements delivered however policyholders prefer to receive funds. Real-time digital disbursements are funds sent electronically and received quickly, without a paper check in the middle. For insurance carriers, this means agent commissions and return premiums move through digital payment processing solutions rather than the mail. More importantly, it means getting funds into policyholders' hands fast, when it matters the most. Raising expectations As younger policyholders account for a larger share of the insurance market, experiences they've grown accustomed to in other walks of life will increasingly become expectations for insurance as well. For many, this translates to being able to complete more transactions on smartphones. Digital payments enable customers to choose a payment method from their phone, receive payment notifications, track payment status, access transaction details, and receive funds directly into an eligible account or wallet. That matters most to the youngest policyholders. When asked for the easiest way to access funds in an emergency, 19% of Gen Z chose a mobile wallet, compared with 5% of Baby Boomers, while only 9% would withdraw cash at a bank, compared with 34% of Baby Boomers. Gen Z's imprint on insurance claims is becoming more pronounced. Today's policyholders want to have insurance claims processed and paid out faster. But they want more. They want the entire journey – culminating in how and when they get paid – to feel as immediate and seamless as any other digital financial transaction. Ray Walsh

items.title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.original_title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.rss_title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.rss_description: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/05/2026 - 17:40 The employment report for September in the U.S. showed a loss of 7,000 jobs in financial services. Insurance, alone, has now lost 90,000 jobs since May 2025. What's going on? I have a theory, and it's not about artificial intelligence. If I'm right, hiring in insurance will stay in the doldrums for a while. Let's have a look. As Insurance Business reports , the industry still employs a massive 2.9 million people in the U.S., but claims jobs are down a hefty 21% over the past year, while life and health is off 4%, P&C down 1.7%, and agents and brokers down 1.1%. The losses are accelerating: The article says, " Insurers lost about 1,900 jobs a month on average in 2025 and roughly 6,900 a month so far in 2026." A thorough analysis in Barron's mostly attributes the job losses to cost-cutting under pressure. Barron's notes that the surge in rates following the COVID disruption has slowed. In addition, government subsidies for healthcare have been cut even as claims costs keep increasing. In the face of pressure on both premiums and expenses, insurers have had to become more efficient, Barron's says. It does say AI has played a role by automating tasks but doesn't treat that as a huge issue just yet (and I've been arguing for months that the fears of job losses to AI are overstated). You could also add the effects of the "silver tsunami" -- the oft-quoted projection by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in 2021 that 400,000 insurance professionals would retire by the end of 2026. Unemployment in insurance remains well below that for the economy writ large -- 3.1%, vs. 4.2% -- so some of the job losses may simply be that companies haven't yet been able to fill the positions left by retirements. But I think there's an overarching issue that gets short shrift if you spend too much time in the details. My Theory My theory boils down to uncertainty. I think economic and geopolitical uncertainty are holding back the economy, in general, and the insurance industry, in particular. And I don't see the uncertainty subsiding any time soon. Tariffs have not only raised costs but, because of their on-again, off-again nature, have slowed investment and the sort of adaptation of supply chains that would ordinarily happen if, say, Canadian lumber suddenly became 50% more expensive. Why spend a lot of money and time if prices might return to normal shortly, whether because of a court ruling against tariffs, because Democrats win control of Congress and assert its power, or simply because President Trump changed his mind? Now add the uncertainty from the war on Iran. Even though oil flows out of the Middle East are improving, Iran retains the capability to attack tankers, to blow up one of the major pipelines being used to skirt the Strait of Hormuz, or to do more damage to the diesel refineries in the region, whose loss has contributed so much to the soaring prices for the crucial fuel. While Trump has repeatedly told us that Iran wants to make a deal and that prices for oil will soon plummet, some of us are old enough to remember how the Iranian zealots acted after taking 66 American hostages in 1979. Angry at President Carter, they didn't release the hostages until minutes after Ronald Reagan became president in January 1981. Who's to say the Iranian theocrats won't treat Trump the way their predecessors treated Carter, declining to make a deal until he leaves office? What is now looking like a blue wave in next month's midterm elections might relieve some of the uncertainty about tariffs, perhaps even leading to serious settlement talks with Iran, but a loss of control by Trump would surely lead to at least a burst of chaos -- perhaps even a sustained stretch. The Democrats are itching to go after him, and he would surely return fire with every one of the many assets at his disposal. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. The Democrats are itching to go after him, and he would surely return fire with every one of the many assets at his disposal. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. items.rss_description: TESTING focus newsletter grant Thu, 10/01/2026 - 15:37 some summary here October 1, 2026 View this email in your browser | Forward to a colleague ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. This month, we're focusing on IT Ops: Change Management FROM THE EDITOR Some two decades into the insurance industry's digital transformation, companies have spent hundreds of billions of dollars on new core systems, cloud migrations, digital portals, and AI tools — but the technology was rarely the hardest part. The hardest part was the people. The people part has long been treated as a supporting act in large technology transformations. But as the pace and complexity of transformation accelerates, that approach is showing its limits. Employees nod along, say they're using the new system, and then quietly find workarounds. Leadership mandates adoption from the top while alignment quietly fractures below. Organizations sprint to the go-live date and then discover that the real work hadn't started yet. Samit Bhandari has watched this pattern play out across the P&C insurance industry for 20 years as a partner at PwC. He's worked with carriers of all sizes through core system replacements, AI rollouts, and full-scale digital transformations — and has seen where these programs succeed and where they quietly go off the rails. He acknowledges there has been improvement—he says the assumption that most large technology programs fail is increasingly out of date. But he says organizations keep making a lot of the same, old mistakes, including the tendency to underinvest in what happens after a go-live, to confuse executive messaging with genuine alignment, and to treat transformation as a one-time event rather than a continuous process. Read the full interview to find out what red flags signal a change management program in trouble, why smaller carriers are often better at transformation than their larger counterparts, and what Bhandari thinks the industry has stopped doing that it should start doing again. continue reading > Reducing the Risk in Change Management Paul Carroll There's often a disconnect in technology adoption that goes unnoticed in business. A leader might mandate the use of AI, and employees will say they're using it—but are they really changing the way they do things, or are they just going through the motions to show compliance? How do you get people on the same page in a big technology transformation? Samit Bhandari First, just in terms of getting everyone on the same page, it's the fundamentals of what we've always said about getting stakeholders engaged—executive, top-down engagement early, right? The messaging from that level through various levels of the organization. And then just the strategic, tactical things—the change champion network and the communication early and often. When you bring in AI—we should be more nimble. read the full interview > MORE ON CHANGE MANAGEMENT Change Management Is Changing by Melissa Palmer Change management can no longer be viewed as a one-time project discipline. It must become an organizational capability. Read More How to Put People First in Your AI Rollout by Tracey Brown "We made a deliberate decision to treat employee confidence as the primary KPI of our AI transformation." Read More Insurance Hiring Practices Hamper Transformation (Part 1) by Amy Radin Insurance companies hire for sector expertise, but transformation demands cross-boundary judgment that traditional filters miss. Read More The Answer to Too Much Technology Is More Technology by Riv Arthur Claudeforce signals a shift from building tools for humans to use and toward creating infrastructure where machines increasingly do the work. Read More How to Build Tomorrow's Insurance Workforce by Afiong Ekong Insurance's talent crisis demands a shift from hiring for past experience to identifying transferable skills and future potential. Ten most read articles on Artemis.bm, week ending October 18th 2026: Hurricane Simon track remained outside of Mexico cat bond parametric trigger zones: Loconte As major hurricane Simon’s path shifted west it remained offshore of the parametric trigger zones related to the $175 million IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 (Pacific) catastrophe bond, according to analysis by Isacco Loconte, an ILS Investment Specialist at asset manager Azimut Switzerland SA. Pillar Capital Management gets strategic investment from SageSure Pillar Capital Management, the Bermuda-based specialist collateralized reinsurance and insurance-linked securities investment fund manager, has secured a new high-profile backer as managing general underwriter SageSure has made a strategic investment in the company. 777 co-founder Wander pleads guilty to $500m+ scheme to defraud lenders and investors Josh Wander, one of the co-founders of investment firm 777 Partners, has pled guilty to wire fraud and securities fraud in connection with a $500 million plus scheme to defraud lenders and investors of the company. Hurricane Isaias insurance industry loss estimated in $2bn – $4bn range: Euler ILS Partners Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, has placed an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion, noting there is the potential for the storm’s losses to add to aggregate structures. Swiss Re says increased reinsurance supply a positive, will align alt capital where it makes sense Speaking ahead of the 2026 Baden-Baden gathering, Leopoldo Camara, Head of P&C Reinsurance Northern, Central & Eastern Europe at Swiss Re outlined that more reinsurance capital is needed in the market to address growing, interconnected risks, while also emphasising that the reinsurer will use its deep risk expertise to align alternative capital where it makes sense. KCC estimates hurricane Isaias wind and surge insured losses at $3bn Karen Clark & Company (KCC) has provided an initial estimate for the private insurance market loss from wind and storm surge associated with recent hurricane Isaias, saying it expects the total to be $3 billion. Lloyd’s issues guidance and expectations for broker-originated reinsurance structures As industry focus grows on designing efficient structures to enable capital to connect with reinsurance risk, Lloyd’s has issued guidance on its expectations for any broker-originated reinsurance structures, which is a strategy that Lloyd’s itself believes is likely to see increasing demand. PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited has now reported that its new US $12 million issuance of insurance-linked securities under Great Wall Re Limited is actually a quota share reinsurance sidecar, the first in Hong Kong, designed to provide protection to its offshore wind power property insurance book on the Chinese Mainland. Evolving captives becoming strategic platforms for attracting third-party capital: Aon Captives are rapidly evolving from risk retention vehicles into strategic capital access platforms, which in turn is beginning to attract third-party capital, according to broker Aon, who emphasises that captive owners are increasingly partnering with external investors to unlock capacity that supports growth initiatives and long-term resilience. ILS investors need to speak up and ask for alternative model views: Karen Clark At the ILS Bermuda Convergence 2026 conference, Karen Clark, CEO and Co-founder of catastrophe risk modelling specialist Karen Clark & Company, urged the insurance-linked securities community and its investors to ask for alternative model views to be included in the deal flow that comes to market. items.extracted_text: Hannover Re's E+S Rück sees more intense catastrophe risk competition, ILS options for clients - Artemis.bm Hannover Re's E+S Rück sees more intense catastrophe risk competition, ILS options for clients - Artemis.bm Hannover Re’s E+S Rück sees more intense catastrophe risk competition, ILS options for clients 19th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Hannover Re’s property and casualty reinsurance subsidiary in Germany anticipates continued strong reinsurance demand at the next rounds of renewals, but notes that rising capacity levels are driving more competition on pricing and terms, while also highlighting insurance-linked securities (ILS) as a complementary offering for clients. With the Baden-Baden reinsurance meetings underway in the country, Hannover Re’s German subsidiary has given its outlook for the regional marketplace, explaining that risks are rising despite moderate catastrophe loss costs of late. Competition is intensifying in many parts of the reinsurance market in the region, as traditional players have growing capital bases. But overall, the company believes demand for high-quality reinsurance protection will remain strong in Germany, with a stable environment overall but characterised by an increasing level of competition to deploy capacity. Thorsten Steinmann, Chief Executive Officer of E+S Rück and the member of Hannover Re’s Executive Board responsible for property and casualty reinsurance in Continental Europe, Latin America and North Africa commented, “The moderate catastrophe losses of the past few years should not obscure what remains a demanding and highly uncertain risk landscape. Natural perils, inflation, cyber risks and geopolitical instabilities are adding to the potential for losses and confronting insurers and reinsurers alike with increasingly complex challenges. “At the same time, many primary insurers have significantly strengthened their earnings and capital position. This builds stability and establishes a good foundation for the upcoming renewals. With certain segments becoming increasingly competitive, we continue to view a disciplined underwriting policy as well as risk-adequate prices and conditions as essential for ensuring the long-term availability and viability of reinsurance protection.” Inflation and costs continue to rise in P&C reinsurance and in clients natural catastrophe reinsurance programmes E+S Rück still sees many of them “adequately priced to reflect the risks.” But rising capacity, thanks to higher capital bases of traditional companies, is “leading to more intense competition and adding to the pressure on prices and conditions.” Recent catastrophe losses from hail events in Switzerland, southern Germany, northern Italy and the neighbouring Alpine regions demonstrate that the underlying risks remain high, the Hannover Re subsidiary said. “In the upcoming renewals, therefore, the individual claims experience, the quality of the programmes as well as risk-appropriate prices and conditions will continue to be decisive factors for E+S Rück,” the company explained this morning. Catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities (ILS) offer alternative and increasingly important capacity solutions. E+S Rück explained, “Alternative risk transfer solutions continue to gain in importance. Insurance-linked securities (ILS) complement traditional reinsurance by providing additional capital market capacity. items.title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.original_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_description: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/12/2026 - 17:45 The recent report that auto thefts fell 21% in the U.S. in the first half of the year reminds me of a friend's carjacking some 30 years ago — surely the shortest in history. My overeducated friend, with degrees from Brown and the Sorbonne, had just added a certification as an auto mechanic and liked cars that required constant tinkering. While driving near his home in Washington, DC, one afternoon, he stopped at a stop sign, and a pedestrian motioned to him that he had a question. Tim rolled down his window, and the man shoved a gun in his face, ordering him out of the car. The man got in, engaged the clutch and drove... two feet. He tried again, but the car stalled after two more feet. He tried a third time. A fourth. He hadn't even made it halfway into the intersection before he jumped out, threw the keys at Tim's chest and ran off. I'd never thought of having a diseased clutch as an anti-theft device but have watched with interest over the years as actual devices have continually improved. They've now gotten to the point that, combined with other factors, thefts fell 17% in 2024, tumbled 23% last year, to the lowest levels in decades, and are way down again this year. The good news for insurers is likely to continue, too. Let's have a look. Some of my optimism stems simply from the steady modernization of the car fleet. Even though soaring prices for cars have encouraged people to hold on to cars longer than in the past, older, more vulnerable cars are steadily being retired, and that trend will continue. In the face of public pressure, companies whose cars were most likely to be stolen have also issued software patches and other updates — as a result, the percentage of car thefts of Kias and Hyundais fell to 14% of the total last year, from 16% in 2024 and 21% in 2023, even as the total of thefts dropped precipitously. Meanwhile, the supply chain has sorted itself out post-COVID, so thieves can't rack up the sorts of profits they did from stealing scarce parts in recent years. The U.S. war on Iran may unsettle the supply chain again, including by pushing sales of electric vehicles during a time of high gasoline prices, but the effects have been muted so far, and I suspect they'll remain so. Law enforcement has stepped up efforts to prevent all sorts of crimes, and car thefts are a visible target at just about all levels of policing. I'm not sure how much more severe enforcement can become, but, especially in a fraught political environment, I don't see that anyone will relax. Potentially the most important — but fraught — factor that will determine how much car thefts keep falling relates to surveillance technology. Flock has built a massive business by installing cameras on roads nationwide that take pictures of license plates and respond to, among other things, alerts from police departments about stolen vehicles. There are lots of efforts to also figure out how to knit together all the images being gathered by dashcams, which are currently in about one in 10 vehicles in the U.S. and which are being adopted quickly. Combining all those feeds could provide real-time intelligence for police departments, making it far easier to catch thieves and creating a massive disincentive for them to steal cars in the first place. But.... We've also seen how surveillance can be abused, as I wrote in August . Flock faces a scandal because dozens of police officers used its technology to stalk current and former romantic partners, and the temptation to use surveillance illicitly will only increase as the technology becomes more powerful. My gut tells me that it will take time, perhaps years, to sort through all the tensions between law enforcement and privacy but that we'll eventually get to the point where some severely circumscribed uses of license plate readers will take another cut out of auto thefts. The privacy issue is one we've mostly navigated with Ring cameras and surveillance cameras on building, so there's a blueprint for progress The bad guys are always innovating, just as the good guys are, but I think the favorable glide path for car thefts should continue. Cheers, Paul P.S. My other bizarro car theft story, this one involving a nephew and an odd situation for the adjuster: While my nephew was visiting DC last year, his Hyundai was stolen off the street by four kids — who drove the car right past him as he was talking with the police officer who responded to his report of the crime. They took the car on joy rides for a few days — as evidenced by the thousands of dollars of traffic violations they ran up in DC and Maryland — then used it in a drug deal that went bad. The car wound up full of bullet holes, and a friend of the kids was shot. Panicking, the kids put the badly wounded girl in the trunk of the car and dumped her in front of her high school. These young geniuses then abandoned the car and tried to run off but were promptly apprehended by school security. (The girl healed fine.) The insurance issue was that the adjuster couldn't look at the car because it was in police custody as a crime scene. So my nephew's insurer kept him in a rental car for weeks until it finally satisfied itself that the car was a total loss and wrote him a check for a new one. My nephew spent weeks unwinding the traffic tickets. He actually had to drive to Baltimore from Philadelphia to appear in court and provide evidence that he couldn't have been at the wheel for the moving violations because he wasn't in Maryland when they occurred. Image Paul Carroll Car thefts in the U.S. tumbled to their lowest levels in decades in 2025, and are down a further 21% this year. The trend is likely to continue, too. items.extracted_text: ADB aims to expand catastrophe bond usage across Asian regions: Kessler - Artemis.bm ADB aims to expand catastrophe bond usage across Asian regions: Kessler - Artemis.bm ADB aims to expand catastrophe bond usage across Asian regions: Kessler 19th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is actively promoting catastrophe bonds for sovereign disaster risk financing across the region, but Thomas Kessler noted last week that this will require cooperation across governments, research and modelling institutions, insurers and the ILS investor base. Speaking in Bermuda at the Convergence 2026 conference last week, Thomas Kessler, Principal Disaster Risk Insurance & Finance Specialist at the Asian Development Bank (ADB) explained that replicating its first successful catastrophe bond issuances takes time and the engagement of insurance-linked securities market participants. As we reported back in April 2026 , the Asian Development Bank’s (ADB) first catastrophe bonds delivered $160 million of capital market-backed parametric earthquake and extreme precipitation disaster risk financing, evenly split between the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan . These were the first transactions issued by the ADB’s own treasury facilities and proved the concept of issuing what it terms Disaster Relief Bonds (DRB), benefiting two of its members and securing them efficient disaster risk financing from institutional and insurance-linked securities (ILS) investors. Importantly, Kessler explained that these catastrophe bonds come with a very clear mandate to deliver any payouts that are triggered during their coverage terms to provide social protection for specific groups. This is not typical of catastrophe bonds, as they more frequently are used to provide reinsurance from the capital markets to insurer or reinsurer sponsors. But in this case the Asian Development Bank designed the risk transfer to have a clear delivery of funding to groups expected to be most affected by the covered natural disaster events. Kessler explained that the cat bonds were structured to have defined payout procedures, that aim to direct funds to vulnerable people and also provide investors with traceable impact reporting. The parametric triggers themselves are designed to reflect affected populations, to ensure delivery of payout liquidity to support the recovery of those in the impacted regions who need it most. As said, the payouts are designed to reach vulnerable households in the covered countries, with that delivered through existing national social protection systems, with the added benefit of reporting and auditing to support traceability for the investors that allocated to the bonds. Kessler told the Convergence 2026 audience, “We actually set up SOPs, standard operating procedures, with many ministries in the countries. And we made sure that children, women, elderly people, people with disabilities, who are registered under the national social protection scheme, would benefit from the payouts, and we set in place reporting and auditing procedures in order to make sure that the household would get the money in case of a payout.” This is an innovative way to both evidence the positive impact of any payout, while also ensuring it goes to those most in need of financial support when disaster strike. It shows a way ILS structures can be designed to provide auditable impact, something that aligns well with the motivations of any sovereign sponsor and with many investors. Kessler said, “This was highly appreciated by most of the investors, because it’s really the first time that we increased the transparency and the traceability of such an instrument, and we provided the investors with measurable SDG impact. “Another unique feature is the triggers of these parametric bonds. So both earthquake and extreme precipitation were linked to the number of affected people, because they are eventually the beneficiary.” Kessler also highlighted that the ADB created a web interface through which both the government’s and the investors could look at the modelling and monitor the impacts of perils, again an innovative feature of these cat bond deals. Having completed its first catastrophe bond issuances, the ADB is now keen to replicate these deals and encourage other regional governments to look to disaster risk transfer as a valuable source of protection. “ADB will further promote disaster relief bonds in Asia and the Pacific. We want to replicate them, take the momentum, and we’d like to have a regional approach,” Kessler explained. “So we look at areas such as the Pacific Islands, which are faced with above average expected loss. We’re looking at Southeast Asia, the ASEAN, which combines large economies, further developed and also very small. We’re looking at the Hindu Kush Himalaya, you have seen the events in Nepal, Bhutan. And of course, we’re going to continue to work in in the CAREC region. “So with this, we will provide opportunities for investors to diversify their portfolios geographically as well as into new risks, and we also hope that investors will get acquainted to new regions.” Kessler closed by saying, “We can’t do it without cooperation between government, between academia, research institutions, science, modellers, structurers and the investors. MDBs, like the Asian Development Bank, can bring them all together. items.extracted_text: Cyber Rates Are Down, Risks Are Up but Small Businesses Slow to Adopt Article 0 Comments The commercial cyber insurance market is strong and growing, but small to midsize businesses may be falling behind as cybercriminals ramp up AI efforts. “Cyber threats are evolving faster than many businesses can adapt, creating significant financial and operational challenges,” said Sean Kevelighan, CEO of the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I). A new members-only issues brief, Commercial Cyber Insurance: State of the Risk , examines the state of the cyber market as well as emerging threats and opportunities. “Cyber insurance is an important part of a comprehensive risk management strategy, particularly for small and midsize businesses with fewer resources to recover from an attack,” Kevelighan said. “However, insurance alone is not enough. Prevention, preparedness and insurance coverage must work together to strengthen resilience and help businesses recover when an attack occurs.” Increasing cyber losses U.S. cyber-related losses reached nearly $21 billion in 2025, up from approximately $16 billion in 2024, according to the FBI’s Internet Crime Report. More than 1 million incidents were reported, compared with 859,532 the previous year. Average cyber claim severity among large U.S. businesses more than doubled to over $4.4 million in 2025, even as claim frequency declined 34% for that segment, according to Chubb statistics cited by Triple-I. Growing premiums, declining rates Global cyber insurance premiums have grown at an annual rate of approximately 5% since 2022, according to Swiss Re. Premiums are projected to reach $16.4 billion in 2026 and $17.1 billion in 2027, with North America accounting for roughly two-thirds of the market. At the same time, cyber insurance rates have declined for four consecutive years, falling approximately 5% year-to-date in 2026, compared with a 13% decline in 2025. Small businesses slow to adopt Despite lower rates and growing risks, adoption remains low among small- and mid-sized businesses, with the market penetration for cyber insurance estimated at just 10% to 20%, according to Swiss Re. These businesses face a double threat, lacking dedicated cybersecurity budgets and advanced defenses as well as cyber insurance. In the face of more affordable coverages, cost may not be the primary barrier to cyber coverage. Misunderstandings about cyber insurance options and benefits may also contribute to the gap, making it critical that the insurance industry help businesses better understand and manage evolving cyber risks and the specific ways in which their organizations may be vulnerable. For example, approximately 15% of data breaches in 2026 originated from supply-chain compromises, with an average cost of approximately $5 million, according to IBM. Increasing AI-related threats AI-powered phishing, impersonation and social engineering schemes are making cyberattacks more sophisticated and accessible. The FBI reported nearly $893 million in losses associated with AI-driven incidents in 2025. While AI is enabling cybercriminals to launch increasingly sophisticated attacks, it is also helping businesses and insurers strengthen defenses, identify vulnerabilities and respond more quickly to cyber incidents. According to IBM, organizations using security AI and automation experienced average breach costs of $4 million, compared with $5.93 million for organizations without those capabilities, a difference of $1.93 million. Ransomware was involved in 48% of data breaches examined in Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report. However, 69% of victims declined to pay ransom demands, due in part to better data backups and cybersecurity planning. Building Cyber Resilience A recent Triple-I/Munich Re US RiskScan study found cyber incidents and AI ranked among the leading risk concerns across five key industry segments, including consumers and small business owners. In a recent Risk Index from insurer Travelers , 58% of respondents said they worry a great deal or some about cyber risks. The concern outpaced those involving economic or geopolitical risks and ranked as the top overall business concern for the fifth time in eight years. These findings reinforce the importance of translating risk awareness into effective protection, Kevelighan said. As AI adoption accelerates, effective oversight, employee training and data security will become increasingly important to managing emerging risks and supporting responsible deployment. “Businesses need to understand not only the financial consequences of a cyberattack but also the proactive steps they can take to reduce their exposure,” Kevelighan said. “Greater education and collaboration among insurers, businesses and cybersecurity professionals are essential to strengthening cyber resilience and helping organizations better prepare for, respond to and recover from an attack.” Triple-I’s Issues Brief also examined the evolving regulatory landscape, including cyber incident reporting requirements and state-level initiatives addressing the use of artificial intelligence in insurance. items.extracted_text: California Hybrid Market Share Hits Record as EV Registrations Decline Article 0 Comments Hybrid vehicles accounted for a record 22.8% of new vehicle registrations in California through the first nine months of the year, a new report shows. However, the Q3 2026 California Auto Outlook , published by Auto Outlook Inc. for the California New Car Dealers Association, shows that zero-emission vehicle registrations fell 26.1% from a year earlier. The report shows strong hybrid demand, as market share rose from 19.5% in 2025 to 24.1% in the third quarter of 2026. Hybrid registrations increased 13.8% through September compared with a year earlier. Zero-emission vehicle registrations fell to 215,467 through September, accounting for 16.4% of California’s new vehicle market. The ZEV market share fell from 24.9% in the third quarter of 2025 to 13.8% in the first quarter of this year before recovering to 17.9% in the second quarter and 17.3% in the third, the report shows. California’s ZEV market share remained more than twice the national figure of 6.2%. The state accounted for 28.9% of all ZEV registrations nationwide, according to the report. Tesla’s ZEV registrations declined 10% through September, but its share of California’s ZEV market rose from 46.4% to 56.5%. Toyota’s ZEV registrations rose 132.5%, while Chevrolet and Ford saw declines of 55.1% and 55%. ZEVs and plug-in hybrids accounted for 59% of small luxury SUV registrations and 42.9% of luxury car registrations, compared with 2.3% of non-luxury passenger car registrations. Hybrids accounted for 45.3% of the non-luxury passenger car segment. The Tesla Model Y was California’s most registered new vehicle model with 86,099 registrations, followed by the Toyota Camry with 52,224. The report also shows California’s used vehicle market outperformed the new vehicle market. Used vehicle registrations rose 2.9% through September, while registrations for used vehicles three years old or newer rose 12%. Registrations for used vehicles four to six years old fell 8%. items.extracted_text: KCC Says Isaias Insured Losses to Be $3 Billion AM Best Calls Storm an Earnings Event Article 0 Comments Catastrophe risk management firm Karen Clark & Co. (KCC) said privately insured losses from wind and storm surge during Hurricane Isaias will be about $3 billion, making the storm one of the most manageable for insurers in recent years. AM Best said the Category 2 hurricane, which came ashore on the Florida Panhandle near the resort city of Destin on Oct. 9, will likely turn out to be an “earnings event” for insurers. Losses will be well below the level to make the storm a capital or solvency event, said the insurance industry rating agency. “The hurricane is not expected to significantly deplete surplus levels in a way that alters industry-wide capacity within the state, thereby avoiding any squeeze that would otherwise lead to a pricing surge,” AM Best said. Claims data from Florida’s Office of Insurance Regulation had not yet been released by Thursday morning. A big factor in the storm’s impact was the unusual nature of its winds. “The strongest winds were recorded on the western side of the storm, blowing water away from the coast, limiting storm surge damage and, thus, flood losses,” AM Best noted. Unlike most hurricanes, the strongest winds, between 105 mph and 117 mph, were recorded near the western eyewall, around Pensacola, according to weather and news reports. A high-rise condo building in Panama City Beach, Florida, lost many of its windows in the storm, similar to what happened to a resort building in Pensacola Beach. (AP Photo/Gerald Herbert) Some coastal areas saw storm surge, but less than had been feared. Panama City Beach, about 90 miles east of Pensacola, saw 5.6 feet of surge, Gallagher Re reported. Inland areas from Alabama to the Carolinas endured some flooding, and 21 tornadoes were confirmed across the Southeast. KCC, which has estimated U.S. storm losses for almost 20 years, said its insured-loss estimate for Isaias includes residential, commercial and industrial properties, and vehicles, as well as business interruption. It does not include National Flood Insurance Program losses. The $3 billion is comparable to Hurricane Idalia, a Category 3 storm that made landfall on a less-populated part of the Florida Panhandle in 2023. Idalia brought storm surge of as much as 12 feet in places, according t o the National Weather Service. By comparison, Hurricane Ian, a powerful Category 5 storm that raked Florida’s southwest coast in 2022, brought an estimated $56 billion in insured losses. “Wind shear increased as Isaias accelerated towards the Florida Panhandle, inducing weakening and causing Isaias to become more asymmetric,” KCC said in its Oct. 15 report. “The strongest winds were displaced to the north and northwest of the eye and the eyewall began to break down.” Still, damage to many homes and businesses was seen in pockets across the Panhandle and in Alabama and coastal Mississippi. Insurance carriers have said thousands of claims have been received, so far. Vexcel, an aerial imaging firm, said its images show about 17,860 structures were damaged by the storm in Florida, Alabama and Mississippi. About 3,141 of those sustained major damage and 631 were destroyed. Before and after photos and video can be seen here . Islam Mahfuz salvages contents of his destroyed mini mart in Milton, Florida. (AP Photo/Gerald Herbert) Inside the city of Pensacola, the storm caused at least $70 million in damage to private property, the city’s mayor told the Pensacola News Journal. It was not clear how much of that property was insured. Escambia County officials said damage to county-owned buildings and facilities had reached $64 million. The cities of Milton and Navarre, east of Pensacola, also suffered heavy damage in spots. Downed trees and severe structural damage to buildings were reported in Milton, KCC noted. Partial and total pull-out of roofs were observed in residential and commercial properties, including single family homes, multi-family homes, motels, and grocery stores. An apartment complex in the city saw most of its roof structure ripped off, and the nearby high school gymnasium lost most of its roof, according to witnesses and news reports. Florida’s Citizens Property Insurance Corp., the state-created carrier that is once again moving toward becoming the insurer of last resort, is expected to absorb the losses. Citizens held about 8,800 policies in the 10-county Panhandle area when Isaias made landfall, OIR data show. By Thursday, Oct. 15, the carrier had fielded 860 claims, most of them from residential properties, a spokesman said. Citizens’ exposure is far smaller than it was just three years ago, as policyholders have moved to primary market insurers after legislative reforms took hold, AM Best explained. “The successful depopulation of Citizens, coupled with a relatively mild hurricane season so far, will keep Citizens intact as Florida’s insurer of last resort,” the rating firm noted. Citizens, which until last year was the largest property insurer in the state, has seen its market share drop significantly. State Farm Group, Progressive Insurance Group, and Berkshire Hathaway Insurance Group now hold the top three spots in the Florida property insurance market, all with market share of at least 6.7%, AM Best reported. “The Florida property-casualty industry is well-capitalized to handle a high volume of insured storm losses and efficiently process claims to help their customers recover as quickly as possible,” Mark Friedlander, senior director of media relations for the Insurance Information Institute, said in an email. items.title: Comp benefits in school bus driver’s fatal crash upheld
items.original_title: Comp benefits in school bus driver’s fatal crash upheld
items.rss_title: Comp benefits in school bus driver’s fatal crash upheld
items.rss_description: A New York appeals court on Thursday upheld workers compensation and death benefits claims involving a school bus driver whose employer argued that an unrelated cardiac event caused his fatal crash.
items.extracted_text: Walter Greek, a driver for Dansville Central School District, was driving an empty bus into the district’s bus garage parking lot on April 5, 2022, when he lost control and struck a parked bus. He was found in cardiac arrest and remained comatose until his death five days later, according to Matter of Greek v. Dansville Central School District , decided by the Appellate Division, Third Department. Mr. Greek had been treated for an irregular heartbeat and cardiomyopathy but had been cleared to safely operate a commercial vehicle. Following the crash, doctors diagnosed brain injuries from prolonged loss of circulation, along with kidney, lung and rib injuries. The self-insured district argued that a cardiac event unrelated to work caused Mr. Greek to lose consciousness and that resuscitation efforts caused his rib and lung injuries. His treating cardiologists testified, however, that chest trauma could have triggered the abnormal heart rhythm. One said it was impossible to determine with certainty whether the arrhythmia preceded the crash or resulted from it. The district’s medical reviewer acknowledged assuming that a cardiac event occurred first. The appeals court upheld the Workers’ Compensation Board’s finding that the injuries arose from the work-related accident or necessary treatment. It also upheld death benefits, citing a medical examiner’s testimony that crash injuries placed additional stress on Mr. Greek’s heart and contributed to his death. The court said that a work-related injury need only contribute to a worker’s death to support death benefits. The district also sought to end Mr. Greek’s injury claim because he died before it could be resolved. The court found that surveillance footage, medical records and an independent medical review allowed the district to contest the claim despite his death. items.extracted_text: Late August Euro SCS and hail event "Raphaela" estimated near EUR 3.3bn industry loss: PERILS - Artemis.bm Late August Euro SCS and hail event "Raphaela" estimated near EUR 3.3bn industry loss: PERILS - Artemis.bm Late August Euro SCS and hail event “Raphaela” estimated near EUR 3.3bn industry loss: PERILS 19th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans The severe convective storm and hail outbreak across parts of western Europe between August 26th and 28th 2026 is initially estimated to have caused nearly EUR 3.3 billion of insurance industry losses, according to catastrophe data aggregator PERILS AG. This severe convective storm (SCS) outbreak that drove significant hail impacts affected parts of France, Germany, Switzerland and Italy from August 26th to 28th 2026, in an event also known as “SCS Raphaela”. A number of large European insurance carriers have noted the potential for meaningful losses from this outbreak of severe and convective storms, with the hail damages particularly impactful and driving significant claims volumes. The event is seen as one of the largest catastrophe insured loss events to ever hit Switzerland, where the hail damage was extreme. PERILS initially estimates the insurance market loss, based on data collected from affected insurers, at EUR 3,296 million, with those losses coming from the property and motor lines of business. A cold front sweeping from west to east across France, Germany, Switzerland and Italy resulted in extensive SCS activity, driven by a low-pressure system named “Raphaela” by the Free University of Berlin, PERILS explained. The storm system interacted with warm and humid air masses from the preceding heat waves across Europe, leading to the formation of numerous SCS systems including supercell storms that produced large hail, destructive winds and intense rainfall. The loss event started in western France on August 26th, before impacting central and eastern France on August 27th, and Switzerland, southern Germany and northern Italy on August 28th. PERILS explained that, “Hail ranging in size from 4-8 cm in diameter was reported in all countries. In France, the region of Besançon in the east was particularly badly affected. In Switzerland, a hail swath stretching from Lake Geneva in the west to Lake Constance in the northeast caused significant damage, as well as impacting southern Germany. In Italy, the northern regions of Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna were the most heavily affected, with hailstones of up to 13 cm in diameter recorded. The hailstorms were accompanied by very strong convective wind gusts and intense short-duration precipitation leading to flash flooding. “There were no storm-related fatalities, but storm damage to property and cars was extensive. As a result, SCS Raphaela is one of the largest Cat losses on record for the Swiss insurance industry. For France, Italy and Germany, the industry losses were less exceptional and remained below the extreme levels experienced in recent years.” Luzi Hitz, Product Manager at PERILS, added, “The Raphaela storms are the second SCS event in Europe in 2026 exceeding EUR 2bn in industry losses. Like the event in mid-July, they originated out of the preceding heatwave which provided ample thermal energy and humidity to support SCS formation. Both events underscore the destructive potential of European summer weather transitions. A primary contributing factor is the ever-warming atmosphere which generates increasing levels of ‘fuel’ for severe convective storms. items.extracted_text: 3M to Argue Australia’s $1.4B ‘Forever Chemicals’ Lawsuit Legally Flawed, Court Hears Article 0 Comments US conglomerate 3M plans to argue a landmark case brought by Australia over contamination from the company’s use of PFAS “forever chemicals” in its firefighting foam is legally flawed , a court heard on Friday. The claim against the Minnesota-based chemicals maker and its local unit is the largest ever brought by Australia, and seeks more than A$2 billion ($1.38 billion) in damages for past and future costs of contamination across 28 military bases where 3M’s products were used. Australia’s case is that 3M knew or ought to have known the foam it made and supplied could damage the environment and harm people, but it failed to warn the government. The foam’s pollution interfered with people’s ability to use and enjoy the water and land around the bases, creating what the government says amounted to a “public nuisance” under Australian law for which 3M should pay compensation. “On Australian authority, the pleaded case does not comprise public nuisance,” 3M’s barrister Philip Solomon said at the first case management hearing for the lawsuit on Friday. “The allegation against us alleged that we, the respondents, had the means to abate the nuisance, that we caused the nuisance, that were responsible for the particular or the special loss associated with the nuisance, and that in a broad sense, we had the ability to control the discharge of the nuisance,” he added. “We will in a number of pages set out why public nuisance as pleaded is not available.” In its defense, expected to be filed on December 11, 3M also plans to question whether another part of Australia’s case — that the company breached consumer protection laws by making misleading claims about the foam’s features and safety — was time-barred because the alleged conduct occurred decades ago, Solomon said. PFAS are a group of manufactured chemicals that are widely used in products resistant to heat, stains, grease and water. Research has linked exposure to PFAS to health issues including liver damage, lower birth weight ⁠and testicular cancer. 3M, which has faced thousands of lawsuits over alleged PFAS contamination, sold the firefighting foam in Australia from 1966 to 2003. Australia has spent A$1.3 billion in dealing with the impacts of the contamination on the bases, including paying A$408 million in legal settlements to affected communities. The defense department has also treated or removed more than 200,000 metric tons ⁠of contaminated soil and treated more than 13 billion liters of water. The case will return to court in December. items.extracted_text: The Crypto Devices Built to Foil Hackers Came With Spies Inside Article 0 Comments At a small cryptocurrency shop in the heart of Kuala Lumpur, a sheet of paper dated Oct. 10 is taped to shutters over the entrance: “Our physical stores are temporarily closed until further notice.” Malaysian retailer CryptoBilis, a reseller of hardware crypto wallets, has become a focal point of an investigation into thefts from devices meant to secure digital assets offline. Customers began reporting missing funds on Oct. 9, and blockchain researchers have estimated losses of over $90 million. Paris-based Ledger SAS, manufacturer of the affected wallets, said on Thursday that a “highly organized criminal group” had fitted some of its devices with hidden hardware. Ledger had previously linked the problem to CryptoBilis, but it is also reviewing reports of implants found in wallets purchased elsewhere — suggesting the problem may extend beyond a single retailer. It’s the latest example of vulnerability in what was once thought to be cryptocurrency’s safest tool. Multiple hacks over the past few months have shown that even physical devices designed to keep digital money beyond the reach of online crooks can be compromised, sometimes before their owners even take them out of the box. “This reveals that crypto storage is an operational risk, not just a cryptographic one,” said Esme Pau, head of capital markets and policy at blockchain security firm CertiK. “Real-world security depends on the entire process.” A Ledger spokesperson said the company is conducting an investigation that includes engaging with local law enforcement and would share more information when available. CryptoBilis did not respond to requests for comment. Social-media sleuths have investigated how the implants work. In their telling , the secret hardware intercepts passcodes sent to Ledger screens, then transmits those keys over cellular connections to hackers, who can then access funds on other devices. This looks like this could be exactly what I’m investigating. Anyone affected, please contact me or open your ledger and send me pictures so we can confirm if there’s a bug in there (pictures: ledger board on top, spy implant below). https://t.co/mg2VRHLRHE pic.twitter.com/0HN3fr7Baq — Mark Karpelès (@MagicalTux) October 9, 2026 Ledger’s hardware features a protection chip, but the attack works around it, according to these experts. As a result, the implants can evade standard security checks until it’s too late. “Protecting against one type of attack doesn’t eliminate the others,” said Aneirin Flynn, chief executive officer of cybersecurity technology firm FailSafe. Ledger represents the latest chapter in a months-long crisis over “cold wallets,” which store private keys and are not connected to the Internet. They were once thought to be impregnable by criminals, but over the summer a software flaw in similar devices made by Coinkite Inc. exposed serious vulnerabilities. That hack resulted in the theft of an estimated $130 million worth of Bitcoin and led to ripple effects across the industry. Soon after, another cold-wallet company called Trezor encountered a data breach through one of its shipping providers that exposed personal information of some 67,000 customers. “People buy hardware wallets to reduce their exposure to online theft, but they’re still dependent on the software, services and people involved in managing their assets,” Flynn said. New Threat Ledger’s latest breach has rattled nerves in a new way. It’s not a software or data-security flaw, but hackers actually cracking open physical devices to steal funds. Even after the company’s update on Thursday, the full extent of the problem remains unknown. Over the years, the company developed a number of devices with different designs, including a new one it’s shopping for $899. Old versions, including the Nano X, sometimes end up with third parties like CryptoBilis who refurbish and resell them. Ben Yorke, who works in the crypto industry from Kuala Lumpur, said he bought a Ledger Flex at a Metapod shop at Singapore’s Changi Airport. Before he got around to setting it up, he noticed that the device looked like it had been tampered with. “I noticed the subtle but suspicious markings on the side, indicating someone may have tried to pry open the back of the device,” Yorke said. He sent it to Mark Karpelès, a crypto founder-turned-researcher, who now runs Tibane Labs . He previously headed Mt. Gox, a digital asset exchange that suffered one of the industry’s most devastating hacks. Karpelès works from Japan, where he received a suspended sentence in 2019 for tampering with financial records related to Mt. Gox’s collapse, and was acquitted of embezzlement. Karpelès was one of the first to post on social media, offering to help victims of the Ledger hack. He examined Yorke’s device and identified a custom connector tapping into the display, along with a cellular chip and SIM card. In an interview, he said the technology was more sophisticated than one might expect. “This is not your guy in a garage putting implants on a Ledger,” Karpelès told Bloomberg. “This is the kind of scale you see in spy movies.” Photograph: A Ledger Flex photo credit: Brent Lewin/Bloomberg Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. items.extracted_text: French Violence Raises Alert as Protests Flare Across Europe Article 0 Comments The violence that rocked France this weekend as cost-of-living protests degenerated into looting and burning nationwide is raising alert levels across Europe, where elections will be held in at least half a dozen countries next year. While France has a long history of street demonstrations, the intensity of attacks on public buildings, shops and restaurants raised fears of repeat action during a campaign featuring both the far left and far right. President Emmanuel Macron promised a “hard line,” yet even as he made a televised address Sunday night, tensions were still flaring between rioters and police in Paris. “This suggests that such extreme violence could become a regular occurrence,” said Bernard Sananes, head of polling company Elabe. He said that there is “no precedent” in recent history of such dramatic unrest in the runup to a presidential vote. Unions have already called for a strike on Nov. 5. Police fire tear gas at demonstrators in Paris photo credit: Wayan Barre/Bloomberg Spending to keep the peace is no longer an option amid deepening concerns over public finances that have sent France’s borrowing costs soaring. A deeply divided National Assembly last week began discussing a budget proposal for 2027 that features about €43 billion ($48 billion) in deficit-cutting measures. French assets fell on Monday as investors pondered the impact of the violence on the nation’s economic and political outlook. Government bonds underperformed most European peers, causing the spread between its 10-year yield and the German equivalent to widen seven basis points to 145 basis points. The euro fell as much as 0.5%. French equities also underperformed, with the CAC 40 index falling 1.2% while the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropped 0.6%. The cost-of-living concerns that were at the root of protests that gathered more than half a million people in France were also on display in other corners of Europe. That includes Italy where parliamentary elections are due to take place in 2027. In Milan, some of the Saturday demonstrations ended in rioting and looting. The violence there worsened on Sunday afternoon, with clashes between police and groups of youth, some of which looted shops. Protests took place also in Belgium and Portugal. Demonstrators in Spain were expected to go on strike next month over housing and wages, just two weeks before a snap general election. Pollster Sananes sees a common thread in these European countries: the failure of public policies to address a sense of inequality. “The problems raised by protesters are all the more acute given the lack of growth,” he said. But the expression of that growing social distress in France, which has been displayed by nationwide student protests the past three weeks over education, has been eclipsed by the violence in the streets. Damage from the unrest will cost “hundreds of millions of euros” to repair, according to Alexandre Bompard, chief executive officer of grocer Carrefour SA and also the head of the French trade and distribution federation. He said in a Sunday interview on LCI that 1,500 storekeepers were affected, with about 20 of his company’s supermarkets looted. Macron, who called the violence a national “shame,” said he understood worries such as a spike in the price of fuel caused by the US’s war with Iran. But, he added, “the country needs order” and he said certain rallies might be banned by regional officials, if necessary. “We will take a hard line against rioters and anyone else who engages in violence,” Macron said. “Seeing the streets of our towns and cities ransacked like this is unbearable,” he added. “Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it.” Macron called on Interior Minister Laurent Nunez to give clarity on planning and intelligence failings that led to the riots, the Elysee said in a statement early Monday. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen said in a speech posted on X on Sunday that the country was “held hostage, between violence and powerlessness.” She blamed the party of her far-left rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon for trivializing violence. “France cannot, must not, and will never get used to such scenes,” she said. Mélenchon blamed police provocation for some of the disorder and disassociated himself from vandals and looters. “What is at stake here is democracy itself,” Edouard Philippe, a former prime minister under Macron and a presidential candidate, said Sunday evening on BFM television. “The ability of every individual to expect that their property and private possessions will be respected and protected by the state.” Further clashes in the streets can be expected over the coming months. A call to strike on Nov. 5 has already been issued by five labor unions in France, demanding higher wages and more funding for public services. They have invited pensioners and high-school students — the first to hit the streets this fall — to join in.
